aboutData.title: About the Data
aboutData.description: The reaction database comes from Dr. Alexander Parkhomov's 2018 analysis of exothermic nuclear reactions between stable nuclides — thermodynamically favorable pathways for nuclear transmutation at low energies. It contains 3,921 fusion, 1,733 fission, and 1,215,374 two-to-two reactions, including neutrino-involved reactions; of these, 1,505 fusion, 818 fission, and 518,657 two-to-two reactions involve no neutrinos. Originally developed as the Nanosoft Package by R.W. Greenyer and P.W. Power for the Martin Fleischmann Memorial Project.

russellChart.title: Russell Chart — Nine-Octave Periodic Table
russellChart.description: Walter Russell's wave-based arrangement of elements into 9 octaves with a serpentine pattern, showing generation (charging) and radiation (discharging) sides with inert gases at the balance points.
russellChart.clickToView: Click any known element to view its properties and isotopes in the database
russellChart.zoomControls: Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, double-click to zoom in
russellChart.waveDescription: Elements plotted as points on Russell's octave wave — amplitude rises through Generation (compression) to Carbon at the apex, then falls through Radiation (expansion)
russellChart.predictionsDescription: Walter Russell predicted several elements before their official discovery, demonstrating the predictive power of his wave-based periodic system.
russellChart.aboutParagraph1: Walter Russell (1871–1963) published his Nine-Octave Periodic Table in "The Universal One" (1926), arranging all elements into a wave-based system of octaves. Each octave has a generation (charging) side and a radiation (discharging) side, with an inert gas at the balance point — the fulcrum of the wave.
russellChart.aboutParagraph2: In Russell's cosmology, matter is created by opposing spiraling vortices of compression (generation) and expansion (radiation). Carbon sits at the amplitude — the point of maximum compression — making it the most balanced and stable element. The serpentine S-curve pattern shows how each octave reverses direction, creating a continuous wave from the lightest hypothetical substances to the heaviest known elements.
russellChart.aboutParagraph3: Russell notably predicted the existence of Deuterium (which he called "Ethlogen"), Tritium ("Bebegen"), Neptunium, and Plutonium years before their official laboratory discovery — validating his wave-based model's predictive capacity.
russellChart.view3DControls: Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom
russellChart.experimentalNote: This visualization is based on Russell's original 1926 chart. Russell's system differs significantly from the modern periodic table — it represents his philosophical and cosmological model of matter rather than the quantum mechanical model used in contemporary chemistry.

mullerResonance.title: Muller Resonance Explorer
mullerResonance.description: Explore electron-proton wavelength resonances between elements using Frithjof Muller's equation L = Z × Cₑ × 2ᴺ, cross-referenced against Parkhomov's nuclear reaction database.
mullerResonance.equationExplanation: L = resonance wavelength, Z = atomic number, C = electron (Cₑ) or proton (Cₚ) Compton wavelength, N = octave number (integer ≥ 0). A cross-particle resonance fixes the octave gap ΔN between the electron and proton ladders; the absolute octave N is free.
mullerResonance.selectElement: Select an element to find its resonant partners
mullerResonance.topGlobalPairs: Top Resonance Pairs Across All Elements
mullerResonance.noResonantPairs: No resonant pairs found at this threshold.
mullerResonance.deltaNTitle: Octave gap ΔN = proton octave − electron octave. Fixed by the resonance; independent of the absolute octave N.

band.label: Wavelength band
band.invalidRange: Enter positive values with min ≤ max.
band.hint: Resonance fixes only the octave gap ΔN. Pick a band to list the octaves N (and wavelengths) where each pair lands.
band.ladderHint: Click a row to see its full octave ladder in this band.
band.lowestNTitle: Lowest electron / proton octave whose wavelength falls in the selected band
band.ladderEmpty: No octave of this pair falls inside the selected band.

mullerResonance.about1: Frithjof Muller's equation L = Z × C × 2ᴺ gives every element a ladder of wavelengths, one per octave N, for both its electron (Cₑ) and proton (Cₚ) Compton wavelengths. Two elements resonate when one element's electron ladder lines up with the other's proton ladder: Z₁ · Cₑ · 2^N = Z₂ · Cₚ · 2^(N+ΔN). N cancels out of this condition, so the resonance fixes only the octave gap ΔN (and how closely the ratio matches), not an absolute octave — if it holds at one octave it holds at all of them. Choose a wavelength band above to see which octaves of each pair land inside it.
mullerResonance.about2: Example: Copper (Z=29) electrons and Iron (Z=26) protons resonate with octave gap ΔN = 11 to within 0.0008%, because 29 × 1836.15 ≈ 26 × 2¹¹. The gap is set by the electron/proton mass ratio (log₂(1836.15) ≈ 10.84). The same match appears on every rung of the ladder: at N = 20 / 31 the shared wavelength is 73.78 µm, at N = 31 / 42 it is 151.10 mm, and each further octave doubles it. Only 8 of 4,186 possible element pairs match to < 0.01%.
mullerResonance.about3: The reaction counts shown are from Dr. Alexander Parkhomov's tables of exothermic nuclear reactions. These counts indicate how many energetically possible reactions exist between each pair, not reaction rates or probabilities. Statistical analysis shows no significant correlation between Muller resonance and Parkhomov reaction density — the database is governed by nuclear binding energies, not wavelength resonance. This tool is exploratory.
mullerResonance.disclaimer: Note: Muller's equation produces elegant mathematics but lacks independent experimental verification of the resonance mechanism. This tool is presented for exploration and hypothesis generation, not as a validated predictive model.

nae.title: NAE Lattice Predictions
nae.description: Elements ranked by electron resonance wavelength proximity to the ~1 nm Nuclear Active Environment (NAE) gap identified by Edmund Storms (JCMNS 41, 2026). Highlighted elements have resonance in the 0.5–2.0 nm range at low octaves.
nae.showNAEOnly: Show only elements with resonance in NAE range
nae.noNAEResonance: No resonance in NAE range at low octaves.
nae.aboutNAE1: Edmund Storms identified that cold fusion (LENR) occurs in Nuclear Active Environments (NAE) — nano-scale gaps or cracks in the metal lattice, typically ~1 nm wide (JCMNS 41, 2026). The unsolved question: WHY does the lattice gap need to be ~1 nm?
nae.aboutNAE2: Muller's equation L = Z × Cₑ × 2ᴺ at low octave numbers (N=3, N=4) predicts electron resonance wavelengths for each element. Palladium (Z=46) at N=3 gives 0.89 nm and at N=4 gives 1.79 nm — the NAE gap falls directly between these octaves.
nae.aboutNAE3: The overlap with deuterium is striking: at proton octave N=20, deuterium has a resonance wavelength of 1.39 nm — right in the NAE range. When the host metal's electron resonance AND the fuel's proton resonance both fall near 1 nm, the system may achieve dual resonance.
nae.aboutNAE4: The known LENR-active metals (Pd, Ni, Pt, Ti) all have electron resonance lengths that bracket the 0.9–1.8 nm range at N=3 or N=4. Elements with no LENR reports (Al, most light elements) miss this range entirely. If this correlation holds, it would be the first quantitative lattice theory for cold fusion.
nae.naeDisclaimer: This analysis combines Muller's resonance framework with Storms' NAE model. Both are theoretical models. Muller's equation lacks independent experimental verification of its resonance mechanism. Storms' NAE gap size is inferred from experimental conditions, not directly measured. Results are presented for exploration and hypothesis generation.

vysotskii-cs-ba.notes: Reported reduction of Cs-137 activity correlated with Ba-138 appearance in growth medium.

vysotskii-mn-fe.hypothesizedMechanism: Net reaction proposed as 55Mn + d → 57Fe via biologically-mediated low-energy fusion

miley-multi-element.hypothesizedMechanism: Broad transmutation product spectrum; no single mechanism proposed (fission of compound nucleus suggested)
miley-multi-element.notes: Catch-all entry: Miley reported a wide product distribution. Ni→Cu used here as the most-cited single pair; ~50 elements were observed.

savvatimova-pd-ag.setup: Glow-discharge bombardment of Pd cathodes in deuterium plasma
savvatimova-pd-ag.hypothesizedMechanism: Multiple pathways proposed including neutron-like processes and electron-screened weak interaction
savvatimova-pd-ag.notes: Savvatimova reported Pd → Rh, Ru, Ag, Cd; Pd→Ag captured here.

savvatimova-pd-rh.setup: Glow-discharge bombardment of Pd cathodes in deuterium plasma

spawar-tritium.hypothesizedMechanism: D + D → T + p reported; not strictly elemental transmutation but an anomalous nuclear process
spawar-tritium.notes: Included as a reference anomalous-nuclear-process claim. Net transmutation is D → T (neutron capture-like).

vysotskii-1996-cs-ba.title: Nuclear Transmutation of Stable and Radioactive Isotopes in Biological Systems
vysotskii-1996-cs-ba.excerpt: Cs-137 → Ba-138 conversion in microbial cultures, reducing radioactivity (1996 onwards).

vysotskii-mn-fe.authors: Vysotskii, V. I. & Kornilova, A. A.

takahashi-tsc-theory.excerpt: Tetrahedral Symmetric Condensate (TSC) model predicts aneutronic 4D → ⁸Be* → 2 ⁴He + 47.6 MeV reaction pathway.

urutskoev-2002-strange-radiation.excerpt: Anomalous CR-39 track patterns observed after Ti-foil electrical-discharge experiments — interpreted as "strange radiation" (2000–2004).

moduleLoad.title: Module Loading Failed
moduleLoad.description: This error commonly occurs on Safari (especially iOS) when content blockers or ad blockers prevent JavaScript modules from loading.
moduleLoad.solution1: Disable Safari content blockers for this site (Settings → Safari → Content Blockers)
moduleLoad.solution2: Disable browser extensions like AdBlock or similar ad blockers
moduleLoad.solution3: Try using Private Browsing mode or a different browser
moduleLoad.solution4: Check if Private Relay is interfering (iCloud Settings → Private Relay)
moduleLoad.solution5: Clear Safari cache and cookies, then reload
moduleLoad.note: Note: This affects approximately 0.6% of users and is usually resolved by disabling content blockers.
